comments.author: mawagoner
comments.text: Screenshots, since they make the discrepancy quicker to read than the logs. Without the workaround. MCP Client node: Input shows only text: hello and the internal tool key; Output shows action: "sendMessage" coming back from the echo server. The agent's reply states it did not pass an action. With the Edit Fields node. Its Input still carries action: sendMessage from the trigger; its Output carries only chatInput and sessionId, and the echo server receives {"text":"hello"}.

comments.author: grinem
comments.text:
Spot-on analysis. Spreading trigger items at the root of `mergedJson` while only rendering `displayJson` in the canvas makes this silent collision a nightmare to trace.

Until core separates execution context from tool arguments in `requests-response.ts`, a quick Code node between the Chat Trigger and the AI Agent stripping `action` will unblock the tool call without breaking the agent:

```javascript
delete $input.item.json.action;
return $input.item;
```

The agent only needs `chatInput` (and `sessionId` if memory is attached). A PR scoping tool arguments strictly to `action.input` would definitely be the right long-term fix here.

comments.author: brunnojob
comments.text:
I confirmed the two code paths in the current source: `requests-response.ts` merges the parent item into the dispatched tool input, while the MCP runtime filters that merged object against the tool schema. That makes a trigger field such as `action` indistinguishable from a model-provided argument when the names collide.

A useful regression test would invoke an MCP tool with an optional field matching a Chat Trigger field (for example, `action`) and omit that field from the model's tool call. Assert that the server receives only the model arguments, while item pairing and parent-item access for expressions remain available. It would also help to assert that the MCP node's displayed input matches the payload actually dispatched, so this class of hidden-input mismatch is diagnosable.
